blocks.text: 07-LPG / landing pages and funnels Goes here. A breakdown of five UX and psychological strategies to reduce "cognitive friction" on e-commerce websites. Covers navigation simplification, bundle pricing psychology, visual hierarchy, and the effective use of images and badges to increase conversion rates and AOV. Not here. • Paid media campaign setup or top-of-funnel ad targeting -> 06-MEA • Automated email marketing flows or SMS strategies -> 09-EML

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details specific, actionable UX optimizations to simplify the customer journey, from reducing navigation clutter to streamlining the cart experience, demonstrating how minimizing cognitive load directly increases conversion rates. modules: [LPG] topics: [conversion rate optimization, CRO, cognitive friction, cognitive ease, UX design, e-commerce, visual hierarchy, bundle pricing, navigation design, A/B testing] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. cognitive friction vs. ease / defining the core CRO concept that high mental effort (due to cluttered navigation or too many choices) kills conversions, while cognitive ease (streamlined design, clear benefits) drives sales; the paradox of choice / identifying that offering too many navigation links (over seven) or too many product bundles (e.g., five instead of three) overwhelms users, and how cutting options actually increases both conversion rate and Average Order Value (AOV); visual selling / leveraging the fact that the brain processes images 60,000 times faster than text by replacing generic navigation text and long product descriptions with scannable icon graphics and lifestyle infographics; benefit-driven copywriting / accommodating the 80% of users who only scan by ensuring that headlines communicate the ultimate benefit ("Why should I care?") rather than just stating the product name; visual hierarchy / guiding the user's attention from the most important element (a bold, large headline) to the Call to Action (CTA) using font size, color contrast, and spacing, avoiding the trap of emphasizing everything; optimizing the product selection process / reducing friction on product detail pages by explicitly stating the exact dollar amount saved on bundles (instead of making users do the math), adding images to bundle variants, and utilizing "Best Seller" or "Most Popular" badges to guide decision-making; the sliding cart drawer / replacing disruptive, page-reloading cart confirmations with frictionless slide-out drawers that offer immediate feedback and integrated cross-sell/upsell progress bars.

The Paradox of Choice Reduction: The specific A/B testing strategy of reducing product bundle options (e.g., from 5 to 3 tiers) to eliminate analysis paralysis, which simultaneously boosts conversion rates and Average Order Value (AOV).

The 7-Item Navigation Rule: The UX heuristic that placing more than seven items in a top navigation menu creates diminishing returns; non-essential links (About, Contact, Blog) should be moved to sub-menus or the footer.

The "Don't Make Them Do Math" Rule: The pricing psychology tactic of explicitly stating the exact dollar amount saved in the headline of a product bundle (e.g., "Save $20") rather than just listing the percentage discount or requiring the user to calculate the difference.
Visual Navigation Menus: The strategy of replacing text-only navigation bars with images or icons representing the product categories, significantly increasing click-through rates.
Skip. The promotional hooks offering free website audits, generic client percentage lifts without the full testing context, and the outro teasing the next video.
Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of cognitive load and visual hierarchy), 85% growth (advanced UX optimization, A/B test case studies, and behavioral pricing tactics). Volume. ~400 words.

Cognitive friction might be destroying your website's conversion rate. So, in this video, I'll explain why that actually is and give you the five-step guide that you can use every single time you create any website page so that you can sleep at night knowing you're not leaving any money on the table. So, let's start by understanding what cognitive friction actually is and why it's important. Cognitive friction simply means how much brain power, thinking or mental effort does someone have to use in order to make a decision and shop on your website. The human brain has something called a cognitive threshold, which is basically how much information can somebody think about and process all at once. If cognitive friction is high and you're above that threshold, that means that your navigation is confusing and hard to use. There's way too much information and there's too many choices. And so people are just frustrated and they're probably not going to buy. What you want to aim for instead is the opposite of cognitive friction, which is also known as cognitive ease. Cognitive ease can be achieved on multiple different levels, including a streamlined navigation, having crystal clear articulation of your benefits, having scannable and digestible text, having an easy product selection process, and having images that complement and reinforce your value prop. When you have all of this, people are way more likely to buy on your website. So, now let's go through my five-step hyperactionable checklist of things that you can do to completely eliminate cognitive friction and instantly increase your conversion rate. The first step to reduce cognitive overload is to actually remove elements on your site, not add more. There's something called the paradox of choice, which basically states that when you give people too much choice, it equals no choice at all. This can happen on multiple different levels on your website. The first low-hanging fruit is by simply cutting down the number of items on your navigation menu. Here's an example of a poor navigation where there's a total of 12 different items that I can choose from, many of which are not even critical to the core conversion action of buying a product. Here's another example where I'm completely overwhelmed by the number of options and I have no idea where to start. My advice is to install a tool called Microsoft Clarity where you can literally see exactly what navigation items people are clicking on. Based on my experience, you can easily cut out two to three items from your navigation because you'll see through Microsoft Clarity that they're getting close to 0% of clicks. Easy example and lowhanging fruit is getting rid of home on your navigation menu. People already know that they can access the homepage by clicking on the logo on your website and this is universally known. The other big thing is if your focus is on conversions, all of these secondary menu items that are not critical to buying products like about, contact, blog, FAQ, all of that can be either entirely removed or put on a submen in much smaller text and much less prominent. My rule of thumb is to never show any more than seven items on the navbar. This is when we start to see diminishing returns and very poor conversions. If you have a lot of products and collections, then I recommend leveraging a nested menu where you're basically limiting the number of products that you're displaying at one time. Also, do not add redundant clicks. Your shop menu does not need to be hidden, right? You can just expose this up front and you're basically saving people an extra click. Reducing elements should also occur on your product pages. This website has so many different elements on the screen that I'm completely overwhelmed and I have no idea what to do next. Compare that to this where it's a nice, clean, and organized layout where I can digest all of the content and I know exactly what to do next. One of my favorite examples is an AB test we ran for a client, Wild Men Drinking, where we noticed on their product page in user recordings that people were getting overwhelmed by the five different bundle options they had. They would either choose one of the lowerpriced options or they were seen in recordings to completely exit the website altogether. And so what we hypothesized is let's cut down from five bundle options to three. And what we saw from that very simple AB test was a 53% increase in conversions and a 13.5% increase in the average order value. So not only were people purchasing more products, but they were also purchasing the higher price options as well, like the three-pack and five pack. The other big thing is to simplify your cart menu. If you look at this example, they have a very poor cart where everything is screaming at me at once. And they've basically tried to add all these CRO best practices with upsells and crossells and it just looks so overwhelming. And the irony is that it's actually probably hurting their conversions rather than helping them. Just strip that all down and go with the basics with a simple cart that shows you the higher tiered options, the items in your cart with some minor upsells and crossells, and then simple next steps. The second step is to use images and icons wherever possible instead of just text. As humans, we're naturally visual creatures, right? The human brain processes images 60,000 times faster than text. Yet, most e-commerce brands don't understand this, and they litter their pages with tons and tons of paragraphs of text that no one ever actually reads. The first critical place to use images and icons is in your navigation menu. Here are some examples of what not to do. These navigation menus are fully textbased and they have nothing exciting or engaging about it. Why should I click further into any of these items and take action? Compare that to these examples that do an excellent job of showing the product in the navigation menu itself through images or icons where I can actually visualize what the product looks like and it's going to make the buying decision for me as a user a lot easier, thus reducing cognitive friction. We actually ran this as an AB test for parcel safety where their original version just had a generic textbased menu. And what we did was we added images and icons and added nested layers. And what we saw was a 60.7% increase in the conversion rate and a whopping 92% increase in the revenue per visitor. Another place you can use icons is what I call the social media icon test where it basically resembles stories on common social media platforms. So basically, you put all of your navigation items out in the open, so you're saving people an extra click, and it's also giving people a visual snapshot very quickly of all of the different product offerings you have. We did this for a pet client as an AB test, and we saw a 72% increase in the conversion rate and an 82% increase in the revenue per visitor. It also generated them an incremental six figures in annual projected revenue, which is absolutely massive considering it's just one small test. Your product images are also crucial. Whenever we look at heat map data on any website, we always notice that the product images are one of the most clicked elements on the page. The big mistake people do is similar to bum where they basically show different angles of their product that adds no substantial value to me whatsoever, and it's a massive waste of real estate in one of the most crucial important sections of the page. What you want to do instead is transform your photos into infographics where you're basically taking your product photos, but you're combining it with scannable value props and USPS on the image itself. We did this for Wild Men Drinking where we took their boring product images and transformed them into custom infographics highlighting all of their different value props, their benefit driven sections, their social proofs, how the product works. And all of this led to a 32% increase in their conversion rate. The last big thing you want to avoid is using large blocks of text that no one is going to read. Chunk all of that content into scannable icons, into bullet points, and into sub headlines. We did this for Wild Men Drinking where we took all of their large blocks of text and put them into scannable icons. And we saw a 25% increase in conversions and a 34% increase in the revenue per visitor. For Fiddler's Green, their entire landing page had large blocks of text. So, we completely transformed it with compelling icons and images and digestible content. And we saw a 158% boost in store orders. As I'm going through all these steps, if you need help in figuring out exactly what's wrong with your website and how to increase your conversion rate, you can apply for a free audit where I'll do a deep dive into all your conversion blockers and give you actionable areas of improvement for your website. Just use the link in the description below and you can apply. The third step is to avoid using vague messaging on your website. Although images and icons are important, you still need to have text to convey the benefit of your product. The big mistake I see a lot of brands make is that they don't understand that people don't read, they scan. In fact, people will only read 20% of the content on your website or page actually read. The other 80% they just scan. So, you need to operate under the framework that somebody will only read the headlines on your landing page or website alone, nothing else. The biggest mistake I often see every single day are generic headlines that are vague, use jargon that have no meaning whatsoever. And the biggest conversion mistake of all time, which is simply explaining who they are and what they do in the headline. I can literally pull up hundreds of examples like these and it's absolutely killing your conversion rate. I cannot honestly believe that people are running paid ads to these. It's literally burning money down the drain. The only thing you need in your headline is why should I care? I want you to put yourself in the shoes of your user and think, what is that one hard-hitting benefit that makes people think and say, take my money? These are examples of pages where every single headline communicates the end benefit and assuming that this is the only thing I read, I actually have an incentive to go and purchase the product just based on the headlines alone. The best headlines in my experience when doing tons of AB testing for our clients are the headlines in which you can quantify the value in the headline itself. So instead of just saying trusted by happy customers, you could put trusted by 700,000 happy customers, which one do you think is going to be more impactful? For Parcel Safety, we completely redid their landing page and took their headlines, which were just generic, and simply explained who they are and what they do, and took it to a completely different level where every headline communicates that end benefit that somebody can receive. Through this new landing page, we saw an 80% lift in conversions. Same thing for Carolina. We completely revamped their page and took all of their headlines to make them benefit oriented and communicating the benefit in the headline itself. and we saw a 157% increase in conversions. Step number four, avoid overwhelming people with poor visual hierarchy. Have you ever wondered why some websites look super chaotic and confusing to look at while other websites seamlessly and naturally guide you to take action? This is due to a concept called visual hierarchy and it's basically the art of guiding the flow of information to the most important elements down to the least important elements using things like font, size, color, weight, etc. For example, here are some pages that are the exact opposite of what you want to do when it comes to visual hierarchy. Everything screams out to you on the page with all different colors, font, sizing. The irony is that in trying to emphasize everything, they've emphasized nothing at all. Compare that to this example where there's a clear flow of information from top to bottom. And the elements that I actually want to stand out on the page actually do stand out. I always like to use this example when explaining visual hierarchy to clients, right? You can see the distinction between all the different elements based on things like font size, weight, color, etc. A great example of visual hierarchy is prepared hero. You can see as you go from top to bottom, the headline stands out on the page and is bold. The body text has slightly less weight and is subdued. The icons and images are clearly separated. And the button stands out on the page and is prominent. To implement visual hierarchy, you just want to logically think what are the most important things I want to emphasize on the page and then actually do that through things like font, color, weight, etc. Likewise, whatever you want to emphasize less, make sure that those are less prominent on the page. Here's a real life AB test example that we did for parcel safety. The old version of their above the fold had no visual hierarchy. The colors clashed with one another, the messaging was subdued, and there was no clear direction of what action they wanted users to take. Compare that to the after version we designed where there's one large headline that stands out on the page and is bold. The badges are on a gray bar that doesn't compete with the main call to action, which is that red button, and there's just overall a clear flow of information from top to bottom. We ran this as an AB test and we saw a 64% lift in conversions and a 72% increase in the revenue per visitor. Step number five, make the product selection process as simple as possible and don't make people think. So, there are a couple different dimensions and levels to this. The first is when you're presenting your different product bundles. While I love Javi's Coffey's website in general, one of the big mistakes that they make is they don't show people exactly how much they're going to save by going with one product version over the other. You never want to make your users do math, right? Trust me, we've tested this a lot. For Wild Man Drinking, we actually ran an AB test where the before version simply just had the savings as a percentage and in small text hidden in the sub headline. And what we did in the after version was we communicated the exact dollar amount that people would save in the headline itself. We saw a 25% increase in the conversion rate and a 28.5% increase in the revenue per visitor just from this one small change. The other big mistake with Javi Coffey's bundles is they don't show people an image of what the product bundles actually are. If they simply added an image of the three-pack, the fourpack, etc., it would substantially reduce the cognitive load to process the differences between all of the different bundle options because of the fact that people process images a lot faster than tech. If you look at Yeti, they do a great job of this by basically showing people what the product looks like, not only when changing color, but also changing the size itself. We actually did this for Wild Men Drinking by adding images to their bundles where they didn't have it before, and we saw a 32% lift in conversions. It seems really trivial, but all of these small differences make a really big difference, especially when you consider how low people's attention spans are. The next big tactic is to guide your users on what actions they should be taking. One of the most effective ways to do this is to utilize badges. The first place you can do this is on your collection page, right? Simply just highlight which products are new, which are the most popular, and the most critical of all, which is best sellers. Naturally, as humans, we want to buy products that other people are already buying and that are already high in demand. And so, from a new user perspective, I'm going to probably gravitate towards those products first. And it's going to reduce the cognitive load in choosing the right product. The next big area badges can be super effective are on product variance itself. You can see with I restore laser, they have the for faster results badge on the second bundle option which basically adds contextual relevance and gives me an incentive to go and choose that option over the first option. And obviously they know what they're doing because that second option is actually an additional cost which is going to increase their average order value. Another great example is perfect snacks where they have the most popular tag which is going to naturally gravitate me towards that option subconsciously and thus lead me to spending more money which means more revenue for perfect snacks. The final critical thing on your product pages to reduce cognitive load is to give people immediate feedback when something has been added to their cart. Take for example this website which reloads the entire page just to notify me that something's been added which is a completely disruptive process. Compare that to this example where as soon as you add to cart it gives you immediate feedback that something's been added through the form of a sliding cart drawer. But it also gives you the opportunity to upsell and cross-ell people directly in the cart itself. If you look at Perfect Snacks again, they reduced a cognitive load by having the progress bar at the very top to indicate what exactly I need to do in order to unlock higher discounts, which is completely brilliant. Now, if you're wondering how I would go about implementing all the things we talked about in this video, click here for the next one where you can watch me performing real life data analysis on an e-commerce brand, showing you exactly how you can pull these same data and basically identify conversion blockers, how to come up with design ideas and run AB test and drastically improve your conversion rate in just a matter of weeks.
